lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Welding codes and standards are the rulebooks that tell you how to make a weld that won't fail. In Africa, many welders learn by watching others, but without codes, you risk building a bridge that cracks, a pipeline that leaks, or a trailer that breaks on the highway. Codes like AWS D1.1 (structural steel), ASME Section IX (pressure vessels), and ISO 9606 (welder qualification) set minimum requirements for materials, procedures, and inspection. They exist because welds fail when they are too small, too cold, or made with the wrong filler. For example, a 6mm fillet weld on a 10mm plate may be fine for a gate, but for a crane support, AWS D1.1 might require an 8mm fillet. If you ignore that, the weld can tear under load. In many African countries, local authorities adopt international codes, but enforcement is weak. That means your reputation depends on you following the code even when no one checks. Knowing codes also helps you win contracts: mining companies, oil and gas firms, and government projects often demand certified welders who can pass tests like the 3G or 4G plate test. This module will teach you the basics of codes, how to read a welding procedure specification (WPS), and how to apply standards in your daily work. You don't need a library of booksâjust a few key rules and the habit of checking before you strike an arc. By the end, you'll understand why a code-compliant weld is safer, stronger, and more profitable.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To work with welding codes, you need the right tools and documents. First, get a copy of the relevant code. For structural steel, AWS D1.1 is common; for pressure piping, ASME B31.3. In Africa, you can buy printed copies from engineering bookshops in cities like Johannesburg, Lagos, or Nairobi, or download PDFs from official sites (some are free for students). Next, you need a welding procedure specification (WPS) and procedure qualification record (PQR). These are documents that tell you the exact settings: amperage, voltage, travel speed, electrode type, and preheat. Your employer or client should provide them. If not, you can write your own using code templates. You also need measuring tools: a fillet weld gauge (to check leg length), a undercut gauge, and a magnifying glass for visual inspection. A digital thermometer or temperature crayons (e.g., Templistik) check preheat and interpass temperatures. For destructive tests, you need a hacksaw, grinding wheel, and bend tester. For non-destructive testing (NDT), you may hire a technician with dye penetrant or ultrasonic equipment. Common materials: mild steel plates (S275 or A36), electrodes like E7018 for low hydrogen, and filler wires like ER70S-6. Always check mill certificates for steel chemistry and strength. In Africa, counterfeit electrodes are commonâbuy from reputable suppliers and look for the AWS classification printed on the electrode. Keep a logbook of your welds, including date, WPS number, and inspection results. This record proves you follow codes and helps you improve. Without these tools, you are guessing, and guessing leads to rejects.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to weld according to a code. Step 1: Read the WPS. Identify the base metal, thickness, joint design, welding process (SMAW, MIG, TIG), filler metal, amperage range, voltage range, travel speed, preheat, and interpass temperature. For example, a WPS might say: 6mm fillet, E7018, 110-140 amps, 20-24 volts, 2-3 mm/s travel, preheat 100Â°C. Step 2: Prepare the joint. Clean off rust, oil, and paint at least 25mm from the weld zone. Use a grinder if needed. Step 3: Set up your machine. Set amperage and voltage within the WPS range. Use a calibrated meter if possible. Step 4: Preheat if required. Use a torch or heating blanket. Check with a temperature crayonâif it melts, you're at temperature. Step 5: Weld. Maintain the correct travel speed and electrode angle (usually 10-15Â° drag for SMAW). Keep arc length short. For multi-pass welds, clean slag between passes and control interpass temperature (max 250Â°C for low hydrogen). Step 6: Inspect. After cooling, use a fillet gauge to check leg size. Look for undercut, porosity, cracks. If the code requires NDT, arrange it. Step 7: Record. Write down the WPS number, your name, date, and any repairs. If a weld fails inspection, you must repair it following a repair WPS. In Africa, many jobsites lack preheat ovens, so you can use a charcoal fire with a steel plate to heat the part evenlyâbut never exceed the max interpass. Always let the weld cool naturally unless the code says otherwise. This method works for any code if you adapt the numbers.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Using the wrong electrode. Many welders grab E6013 because it's easy, but for code work, low hydrogen E7018 is often required. Fix: Check the WPS. If it says E7018, use it, and store it in a heated rod oven (or a sealed container with silica gel). Mistake 2: Ignoring preheat. On thick steel (over 25mm), cold welding causes cracking. Fix: Preheat to 100-150Â°C using a torch or oven. Test with a temperature crayon. Mistake 3: Too fast travel. This causes narrow, convex beads and lack of fusion. Fix: Slow down and watch the puddle wet out at the edges. Mistake 4: Wrong fillet size. A 6mm fillet on a 10mm plate may be under-sized for the load. Fix: Use a fillet gauge. If the leg is 5mm, add another pass. Mistake 5: Poor interpass temperature control. Welding continuously can overheat the steel, causing grain growth and reduced toughness. Fix: Let it cool to below 250Â°C between passes. Mistake 6: No cleaning between passes. Slag inclusions cause rejects. Fix: Chip and brush every pass. Mistake 7: Skipping documentation. Without a WPS and records, you can't prove compliance. Fix: Keep a logbook and copy of the WPS on site. Mistake 8: Using damaged cables or loose connections. This causes voltage drop and poor welds. Fix: Inspect cables daily. In Africa, power fluctuations are commonâuse a voltage stabilizer if possible. If a weld fails inspection, don't just grind and re-weld; find the root cause. Was it amperage? Travel speed? Moisture in electrode? Fix the cause, then repair. Remember: codes are minimums, not maximums. Doing it right the first time saves money and lives.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Welding codes also cover safety. The main hazards are electric shock, fumes, arc eye, burns, and fire. For electric shock, ensure your machine is grounded and use dry gloves. Never weld in wet conditions. For fumes, especially with galvanized steel or stainless, use a respirator and ventilate the area. In Africa, many workshops are open-air, which helps, but still position yourself upwind. Arc eye comes from UV radiationâalways wear a welding helmet with at least a shade 10 lens for arc welding. For gas welding, shade 5. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby and a bucket of sand. Never weld near flammable liquids. Best practice: follow the code's safety section (e.g., AWS Z49.1). Wear leather gloves, apron, and safety boots. Use screens to protect others. For confined spaces, use a gas monitor and a spotter. Also, codes require welder qualification. You should test every 6 months or when you change process. In Africa, many welders skip this, but a qualified welder can command higher pay. Keep your certification card. Another best practice: use the correct amperage. Too high burns through; too low causes lack of fusion. Check the WPS. Finally, maintain your equipment. Replace worn liners, tips, and nozzles. A clean machine runs cooler and welds better. If you work at height, use a harness. If you weld in a tank, have a rescue plan. Safety is not optionalâit's part of the code. A safe welder is a productive welder.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: For this exercise, you will make a fillet weld on a T-joint and check it against a code. You need: two steel plates 10mm thick, 100mm x 50mm each; E7018 electrodes 3.2mm; a SMAW machine; a fillet weld gauge; a wire brush; a chipping hammer; a temperature crayon (100Â°C); and a hacksaw. Step 1: Clean the plates. Step 2: Tack weld the plates to form a T. Step 3: Preheat to 100Â°C using a torch. Check with crayon. Step 4: Set amperage to 120A (within WPS range). Step 5: Weld a 6mm fillet along the joint. Use a 10-15Â° drag angle, short arc. Step 6: Let it cool. Clean slag. Step 7: Measure the fillet leg with a gauge. It should be 6mm Â±1mm. If under, add a pass. Step 8: Inspect for undercut (max 0.5mm), porosity, cracks. Step 9: Cut the weld cross-section with a hacksaw. Polish with a file. Look for fusion at the root. If there is lack of fusion, your travel was too fast or amperage too low. Step 10: Write a short report: WPS number, amperage, preheat, leg size, defects found, and repair action. This exercise mimics a real code test. In Africa, you can do this in a workshop with minimal tools. Repeat until you can consistently pass. Then try a 3G (vertical) test. That's what employers pay for.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of welding codes and standards?
options: A) To make welding more expensive
B) To ensure welds are safe and reliable
C) To replace the need for training
quiz.explanation: Codes set minimum requirements to prevent failures and protect lives.

quiz.q: Which code is commonly used for structural steel welding?
quiz.explanation: AWS D1.1 is the structural steel welding code.

quiz.q: What does WPS stand for?
quiz.explanation: WPS is the document that specifies welding parameters.

quiz.q: Why is preheat used in welding thick steel?
options: A) To make the weld prettier
quiz.explanation: Preheat slows cooling and reduces the risk of hydrogen cracking.

quiz.q: Which electrode is low hydrogen?
quiz.explanation: E7018 has a low hydrogen coating, reducing cracking risk.

quiz.q: What tool checks fillet weld leg size?
quiz.explanation: A fillet weld gauge directly measures leg length.

quiz.q: What is the maximum interpass temperature for low hydrogen electrodes?
quiz.explanation: Exceeding 250Â°C can reduce toughness.

quiz.q: What causes undercut in a weld?
options: B) Too high amperage or too fast travel
quiz.explanation: High heat or fast travel melts the base metal edge without filling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a PQR?
options: A) To record procedure qualification test results
quiz.explanation: PQR documents that a WPS has been tested and qualified.

quiz.q: Which safety gear protects against arc eye?
options: B) Welding helmet with proper shade
quiz.explanation: The helmet lens filters UV radiation that causes arc eye.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding according to a code?
quiz.explanation: The WPS gives all required parameters.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean between passes?
quiz.explanation: Slag left between passes causes defects.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when welding in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Counterfeit electrodes are common and fail code requirements.

quiz.q: What does NDT stand for?
quiz.explanation: NDT inspects welds without damaging them.

quiz.q: Which gas is a hazard when welding galvanized steel?
quiz.explanation: Zinc fumes cause metal fume fever.

quiz.q: What is the correct travel speed for a 6mm fillet with E7018?
quiz.explanation: Typical travel speed is 2-3 mm/s for that size.

quiz.q: What should you do if a weld fails inspection?
options: B) Grind and re-weld without finding cause
C) Find root cause and repair per WPS
quiz.explanation: Repair must follow a qualified procedure.

quiz.q: Why keep a welding logbook?
quiz.explanation: Records show you followed the code.

quiz.q: What is the minimum shade for arc welding helmet?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10 or higher protects against UV.

quiz.q: Which document tells you the amperage range?
quiz.explanation: The WPS specifies all welding parameters.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of porosity?
quiz.explanation: Moisture creates gas pockets in the weld.

quiz.q: How often should a welder requalify?
quiz.explanation: Codes often require requalification every 6 months.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a temperature crayon?
quiz.explanation: Crayons melt at specific temperatures.

quiz.q: Which code covers pressure vessels?
quiz.explanation: ASME Section IX covers welding qualifications for pressure vessels.

quiz.q: What is the maximum allowed undercut for many codes?
quiz.explanation: Typical limit is 0.5mm for critical welds.

quiz.q: Why use a voltage stabilizer in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Unstable voltage affects weld consistency.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes contaminants before welding.

quiz.q: What does a fillet weld gauge measure?
quiz.explanation: It measures the leg of a fillet weld.

quiz.q: What is a common defect when travel speed is too fast?
quiz.explanation: Fast travel doesn't allow proper fusion.

quiz.q: Why is it important to follow codes even if not enforced?
options: A) To increase reputation and safety
quiz.explanation: Codes ensure safety and build trust with clients.
